n: This lecture is devoted to poisonous substances isolated with polar solvents. The plan is as follows: poisonous substances isolated from the specimen with polar solvents, and the general methods of isolation with polar solvents. Key terms: extraction, organic solvent, pH conditions, electrolyte, extractive substances, number of extractions and polar solvent. The isolation methods fall into two groups: acidified alcohol, that is, the Stas-Otto method, and acidified water, that is, the methods of Dragendorff, Shvaikova-Vasilyeva and Kramarenko.

This group of medicinal and poisonous substances is extremely diverse in chemical structure and includes a great many compounds. They include organic acids, polyhydric phenols, polynitro compounds, aniline, PABA derivatives, barbiturates, alkaloids and nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds. These substances may have acidic, basic or neutral properties. Therefore they are extracted from aqueous solution with an organic solvent. That is, although the structure differs, the route of isolation is common.

t: The 28 substances examined in a complete analysis
n: In a complete chemical-toxicological analysis, the expert chemist must test for 28 substances of this group. According to the book, the composition of these substances is as follows: 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds. In all there are 28 substances. The table shows each group and the number of substances in it.

Now, the list of these substances. Barbiturates: barbital, phenobarbital, barbamyl, etaminal sodium, cyclobarbital, that is, phenodorm, hexobarbital, that is, evipan, and benzonal. Alkaloids: morphine, codeine, dionine, heroin, hydrocodone, papaverine, strychnine, atropine, hyoscyamine, scopolamine, cocaine, pachycarpine, anabasine, nicotine and quinine. Nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds: promedol, aminazine, diprazine, tisercin, mazheptil, triftazine, imizine and its analogues.

Medicinal substances in the crystalline state are isolated from the specimen with acidified water and acidified alcohol. In an acid medium, barbiturates and alkaloids form salts through the nitrogen atom in the molecule and pass into the aqueous or alcoholic solution. In the acidified alcohol method, ethyl alcohol acidified with oxalic or tartaric acid is used; this method is associated with the names of Stas and Otto. Alkaloid salts dissolve well in alcohol. In the acidified water method, water acidified with a mineral or organic acid is used; it was proposed by Uslar and Erdman with hydrochloric acid.

We consider the chronology of the methods. The acidified alcohol method was proposed around the 1840s. In 1851 Stas applied it to the isolation of alkaloids. In 1856 F. Otto introduced a modification to the method. In 1861 Uslar and Erdman used acidified water. Then the method developed: in 1942 Stepanov and Shvaikova, in 1946 Vasilyeva, and in 1956-1961 Kramarenko improved the method.

Stas's method. The acidified alcohol method was proposed in 1851 by the Belgian scientist J.S. Stas for isolating alkaloids from specimens in forensic chemical examination. The basis of the method is that alkaloids as salts dissolve well in alcohol. Ethyl alcohol acidified with oxalic or tartaric acid was poured over the specimen. Remember: in this original form the isolate was not purified of foreign substances.

In 1856 F. Otto introduced a modification to the method and proposed purifying the alcoholic isolate. After that the method began to be called the Stas-Otto method. Later further modifications were made to the method: acidification with various mineral acids, alkalinisation with various alkalis, and replacement of organic solvents. So the Stas-Otto method was developed while retaining the basic idea.

The stages of the Stas-Otto method. First the biomaterial is steeped several times with ethyl alcohol acidified with oxalic acid and left for 1 day. The alcoholic solutions are combined and evaporated at 35 °C until a small amount remains. To the isolate, in syrup form, 96 % ethyl alcohol is added to precipitate foreign substances. Then it is diluted with warm water, extracted 3 times with diethyl ether, and the ether layer is discarded. The acid alcoholic solution is made alkaline with ammonia or sodium bicarbonate, extracted 3 more times with ether, and the alkaloids are examined.

t: Stas's method: details in the qualification material
n: Now the details of Stas's method in the qualification material. The minced biological specimen is mixed with twice the amount of 96° ethyl alcohol, and a strongly acid medium is formed with oxalic acid. The mixture is heated for a long time on a water bath at about 70-75 °C. After the alcoholic solution is separated, the process is repeated with 96 % alcohol. The dry residue is dissolved in a little water, sulphuric acid is added, then it is made alkaline with sodium bicarbonate and extracted several times with ether.

t: Evaluation of the acidified alcohol method
n: We evaluate the acidified alcohol method. Its drawbacks: it takes a long time, its sensitivity is low, expensive alcohol is needed, and results are variable. According to the qualification material the analysis drags on for 8-10 days, and more than 500 ml of pure ethyl alcohol is used for one analysis. Its convenience is that a substance can be isolated even from a putrefied specimen. Because the purification takes place in the presence of alcohol, almost no emulsion forms.

The acidified water method. The first to use acidified water to isolate alkaloids from a biological specimen, in 1861, were Z. Uslar and L. Erdman. They proposed acidifying the specimen with hydrochloric acid. Later many authors proposed phosphoric acid, sulphuric acid and other mineral and organic acids for acidification.

Dragendorff's method. The specimen is acidified with sulphuric acid, and the aqueous solution is evaporated to a syrup. The syrup is steeped for 24 hours in 96 % alcohol and filtered. The filtrate is mixed with water and extracted with petrol, petroleum ether and chloroform. The aqueous layer is made alkaline with ammonia and extracted again with petrol and isoamyl alcohol. The extracts are combined and examined for alkaloids.

The drawbacks of Dragendorff's method. Heating and evaporating the sulphuric acid isolate leads to the hydrolysis of most ester-type alkaloids. As a result, an impure residue is obtained. Moreover, purification by extraction with various solvents causes a partial loss of substances. That is, the method has a problem of both purity and loss.

The origin of the Shvaikova-Vasilyeva method. The researches of A.V. Stepanov, M.D. Shvaikova, A.A. Vasilyeva and V.F. Kramarenko are of great importance for the isolation of alkaloids. In 1942 Stepanov and Shvaikova developed a method of isolating alkaloids from plant parts with water acidified with oxalic acid. In 1946 A.A. Vasilyeva applied the method to isolating alkaloids from cadaver organs. The method is called the method of Shvaikova and Vasilyeva and is important as a rapid method.

We evaluate Vasilyeva's method. Its advantage: the method is performed quickly and does not require expensive reagents. According to the qualification material, from examining the specimen to obtaining the chloroform isolate takes 3-4 hours, so the method is also called the accelerated method. Its drawback: it is difficult to isolate substances that do not dissolve in acidified water. Also, toxicologically significant substances cannot be isolated completely from a putrefied specimen, because a stable emulsion forms in the extraction.

Kramarenko's method. In 1956-1961 V.F. Kramarenko, with his students, improved the acidified water method. He proposed taking into account the pH of the specimen's medium, the character of the organic solvents and the influence of electrolytes. Centrifugation was proposed instead of filtration. According to the qualification material, Kramarenko's group studied the influence of pH and solvent in isolating more than 50 alkaloids and their synthetic analogues.

The pH basis of Kramarenko's method. It was taken into account that alkaloids in the body are altered by hydrolysis, oxidation and reduction and form with proteins a complex insoluble in water. Alkaloids bind well to proteins in a weakly acid medium, at pH 4-5, and this property strengthens as pH rises. In the living body pH is 7.3-7.5, in a cadaver about 6.2. To break this complex, the pH is brought to 2.5-3.

Kramarenko's method, the steeping stage. 100 g of specimen is covered with 0.02 N sulphuric acid solution until the pieces are submerged. Then with 20 % sulphuric acid the pH is brought to 2-2.5 and it is left for 2 hours, the pH of the medium being checked continually. The aqueous layer is poured off. The specimen is steeped twice more in the same way, for 2 and 1 hours.

Kramarenko's method, centrifugate and deproteinisation. The acid aqueous solutions are combined and centrifuged. Crystalline ammonium sulphate is added to the centrifugate until a saturated solution forms. After 1-2 hours the precipitate is centrifuged. The precipitate is steeped with 0.02 N sulphuric acid, and its centrifugate is added to the main centrifugate, pH 2.0-2.5. The combined centrifugate is extracted twice with 40 ml of ether. The ether extract is discarded or examined for substances of acidic character.

Kramarenko's method, alkalinisation and extraction. To the acid aqueous solution, 20 % sodium hydroxide is added to pH 8.5-9.0. The pH changes because of the ammonia liberated in the reaction: ammonium sulphate and two molecules of sodium hydroxide form two molecules of NH4OH and sodium sulphate. Then it is extracted 3 times with chloroform. As a side effect of the alkali, morphinate is not formed from morphine.

t: Kramarenko's method: test for iodide ion
n: Kramarenko's method, test for iodide ion. The alkaline aqueous isolate left after extraction is acidified with acid until an acid medium forms. Sodium nitrite is added and it is tested for iodide ion, pachycarpine being meant here. If iodide ion is present, when 1 ml of chloroform is added and the mixture is shaken, the chloroform layer turns red-pink.

We repeat the important figures. In the Stas-Otto method the alcoholic solutions are evaporated at 35 °C, and 96 % alcohol is added to the syrup isolate. In Kramarenko's method 100 g of specimen is taken, steeping takes place at pH 2-2.5, and extraction with ether is done twice with 40 ml. The acid solution is made alkaline with 20 % NaOH to pH 8.5-9.0 and extracted 3 times with chloroform.

We evaluate Kramarenko's method. The method is sensitive, poisonous substances are isolated completely, it is performed relatively quickly, and the reagents are easy to obtain. On the basis of Kramarenko's method, moderate conditions have also been applied to the Stas-Otto and Vasilyeva methods. Its drawback is that substances of acidic character, for example barbiturates, are isolated only partially and in small amounts.

We compare the polar solvent methods by table. In the Stas-Otto method acidified ethyl alcohol was used, in Uslar-Erdman water with HCl, in Dragendorff sulphuric acid. The Shvaikova-Vasilyeva method is based on water with oxalic acid, and Kramarenko's method on 0.02 N H2SO4 and centrifugation. Kramarenko's method is sensitive, poisonous substances are isolated completely, and it is performed relatively quickly. In the table the important feature of each method is shown separately.

Current practice. The specimen is isolated with polar solvents at pH 2.5-3.0, the Stas-Otto, Vasilyeva and Kramarenko methods being taken as the basis. From the aqueous isolate, alkaloids are extracted at pH 9. As a result the chemist has two isolates: acid and alkaline. The solvent is more often chloroform, sometimes ether.

t: Substances examined in the two isolates
n: Let us see what is examined in the two isolates. The isolate obtained in an acid medium is examined for barbiturates, neutral substances, for example phenacetin, and organic acids, salicylic and picric. In this same isolate weakly basic alkaloids are also examined: caffeine, theobromine, theophylline, papaverine, narcotine and strychnine. From the isolate obtained in an alkaline medium, alkaloids and their synthetic analogues are examined.

Liquid alkaloids: anabasine, nicotine, pachycarpine, coniine and arecolines. As bases they are oily liquids with a characteristic smell, sufficiently volatile and readily soluble in organic solvents. Their salts are readily soluble in water, while the bases dissolve in organic solvents and are distilled with steam as an azeotropic mixture. Therefore they are isolated by steam distillation in an alkaline medium. The distillate is made alkaline and extracted with chloroform.

Now the alkaloid yield, that is, the percentage isolated. For morphine, 18-21 % by the Stas-Otto method, 21-24 % by Vasilyeva's method, 47-51 % by Kramarenko's method. For codeine, Stas-Otto 24-25 %, Vasilyeva 33-40 %, Kramarenko 59-63 %. According to the table in the qualification material, Kramarenko's method is the most convenient.

Yield of cocaine and quinine. Cocaine: 17-19 % by the Stas-Otto method, 25-32 % by Vasilyeva's method, 53-56 % by Kramarenko's method. Quinine: Stas-Otto 14-18 %, Vasilyeva 23-41 %, Kramarenko 63-69 %. Remember: for quinine by Vasilyeva's method the range is wide, 23-41 %.

Yield of strychnine and brucine. Strychnine: 22-26 % by the Stas-Otto method, 30-34 % by Vasilyeva's method, 50-56 % by Kramarenko's method. Brucine: Stas-Otto 29-32 %, Vasilyeva 27-33 %, Kramarenko 51-55 %. For brucine, the acidified alcohol method gave a slightly higher yield than Vasilyeva's method.

Barbiturates and polar solvent methods. Barbiturates, apart from thiopental sodium, are solid crystalline substances: readily soluble in ether, less so in chloroform and alcohol, and poorly soluble in water. Therefore extracting barbiturates with ether gives a good result, and they sublime at a high temperature. For barbiturates the methods for alkaloids were used for a long time, and in recent years special methods are used.

t: Barbiturates: the Gruss-Hardy and Valov methods
n: The Gruss-Hardy and Valov methods for barbiturates. The Gruss-Hardy method is intended for benzonal: the specimen is acidified with HCl to pH 2, saturated with ammonium sulphate, and a mixture of chloroform and alcohol is added. The chloroform layer is treated with phosphate buffer pH 7.4: the chloroform layer is tested for benzonal, and the buffer layer for benzoic acid. In Valov's method the specimen is treated with alkaline water to pH 10, Na tungstate and H2SO4 are added to the aqueous layer to bring it to pH 2, the precipitate is centrifuged, and the barbiturates are transferred into ether.

t: Barbiturates: oxalate method, blood and urine
n: The oxalate method for barbiturates, and isolation from blood and urine. In the method of Shvaikova and her students, the specimen is extracted with water acidified with oxalic acid, pH 2, and the aqueous solution is extracted with chloroform. The isolate is purified by shaking with 0.1 N alkali, the aqueous layer is acidified to pH 2 and extracted again with chloroform. In this, 20-30 % of the barbiturate is isolated. From blood and urine, extraction into chloroform with HCl at pH 2 is performed, re-extraction with alkali at pH 13 is carried out, and determination is by spectrophotometry in borate buffer at pH 10.

We compare the barbiturate yield by method. The figures are given in the order of the Stas-Otto, Vasilyeva, Kramarenko, Valov and Popov methods. Barbamyl: 45, 19, 7, 35, 43. Barbital: 32, 14, 20, 26, 28. Hexenal: 16, 31, 5, 32, 42. Phenobarbital: 48, 29, 7, 35, 38. Cyclobarbital: 19, 20, 2, 30, 40. Etaminal: 41, 18, 4, 27, 43. Thiopental: 11, 17, no value for Kramarenko's method, 16, 20. So in Kramarenko's method part of the barbiturates may be precipitated with ammonium sulphate, and therefore they cannot be isolated completely.

The acetone-water method. In an acid medium the specimen is steeped and extracted three times with acetone-water, the acetone-water solutions are combined and centrifuged. The centrifugate is saturated with sodium chloride until the acetone layer separates. The acetone layer is separated and the acetone is evaporated. The aqueous part is extracted 3 times with chloroform. The residue is purified by TLC, and hexamidine and phenobarbital are separated from each other.

t: Choice of method and gaps the book does not cover
n: The question of choosing a method. The only drawback of the acidified water method is that when a specimen that has stood a long time and putrefied is extracted with chloroform, a stable emulsion forms. Therefore the forensic chemist chooses one of the two methods according to the state of the physical evidence. The acidified alcohol method gives little emulsion with a putrefied specimen, while the aqueous method is quick and sensitive.

We conclude. Polar solvents: acidified alcohol, that is, Stas 1851 and Otto 1856, and acidified water, that is, Uslar-Erdman 1861, Dragendorff, Vasilyeva and Kramarenko. Kramarenko's method: 100 g of specimen, 0.02 N H2SO4, pH 2-2.5, centrifugation, ammonium sulphate, three extractions with chloroform at pH 8.5-9.0. In current practice the specimen is isolated at pH 2.5-3.0, and the two isolates, acid and alkaline, are analysed separately. For self-check: compare the methods and explain the pH basis of Kramarenko's method.
